author: Nina Thompson
title: Residents bring array of issues to Sen. Rest listening session - NewsBreak
text:
By Nina Thompson ,
17 hours ago
Minnesota Sen. Ann Rest, DFL representative of New Hope, Golden Valley, Crystal, Robbinsdale and parts of Plymouth, announced she will retire after over 40 years in the state legislature.
After the announcement, she scheduled a series of listening sessions for constituents, meeting at 11 a.m. Saturday in a secondary dining room at the coveted Frankie’s Pizza in New Hope.
Listening sessions give Rest the opportunity to hear local constituents express their frustrations and raise questions about various government matters.
On Oct. 4, residents brought local, national and international topics for Rest to absorb by the next legislative session in February of 2026.
The government shutdown
What happens in the pearly chambers of the United States Capitol, although over a thousand miles away, still impacts those residing in Minnesota’s Senate District 43.
The last government shutdown in 2019 was the result of an impasse over funding President Trump’s wall along the U.S.-Mexico border with taxpayer dollars.
For the current shutdown, which began on Oct. 1, Congress must decide whether to continue health insurance tax credits for millions of Americans through the Affordable Care Act. Congress democrats are also pushing to reverse Medicare slashes from Trump’s “Big, Beautiful Bill” passed earlier this year.
“I’m concerned about how the (Affordable Care Act) premium tax credits will drive up insurance costs,” a Robbinsdale resident and parent said at the session.
“What can the legislature do to keep premiums affordable? ... What do we do when this (shutdown) extends beyond 35 days? What does Minnesota do legislatively?” he asked.
Rest, with 40 years of experience in the legislature and an emphasis on tax equity, remains hopeful. “I just personally don't believe that Minnesota Republicans and Democrats are going to allow us to be devastated in that way, regardless of what the federal government does,” she said. “I think we'll come together on something.”
On Gun violence and school shootings
In September, a Senate committee of Democrats and Republicans was formed to discuss early legislative proposals preventing gun violence across the state.
At the initial meetings, which accrued over six hours of debate and testimony, Sen. Zayneb Mohamed (DFL-Minneapolis) proposed an assault-weapon and high-capacity magazines ban, while Republican senators brought forward school-hardening and mental health perspectives, all in the pursuit of limiting gun deaths.
The philosophical debate on whether the weapons or their wielders cause gun deaths is active on both large and local scales.
Rest was not a member of the committee, but she made her stance clear: “If I have to vote for a ban on assault weapons and high-capacity magazines, I'm going to take it,” Rest said to the group of constituents. “Whether it's in a special session, whether it's an amendment on the floor, wherever it is. I'm going to take it."
“I also would support mental health. But those two have to go together,” she said, in a deliberate way that works hand-in-hand with weapons restrictions.
“Mental health dollars are not just going to go to social workers in Hennepin County. They're going to go to any number of non-government organizations, and we're going to have the same opportunity for fraud in treating people with mental illness,” she said.
“Maybe a third of the people in this room have had counseling for emotional distress, mental distress. And you know what? Not a single one of us kills.”
Spirited debates came from the gun violence discussion, as well as differences in thought about Israel’s occupation and assault on Gaza.
But at the end of the session, Rest left constituents with a reminder: “I really am so grateful for how tolerant you are to one another… we need to do more of that,” she said. “We need to do it with our friends, our family members, our communities. And I salute all of you for that.”
